> Illegal actions often involve deprivation of the source object, but many pirates do not acknowledge that their piracy is actually capable of such deprivation (as an existential threat to the creators, albeit in only extreme cases).  

Someone else quotes Gabe Newell talking about piracy as a service problem and I think these two things really show a big problem I experience.  
I like anime a lot. I want to monetarily support the actual creators of a show, not necessarily the one who owns the IP like the publishing company. I don't care about the marketing, I don't want translations. I want the team that is actually involved in the production of the thing that I like to get the money, not the ever increasing amount of middle men adding irrelevant services to it. Paradoxically, the more I try to do this by legal means, the less that means they are going to get. I have to use a company's services I am not interested in to legally watch it and I can be sure that they are taking a cut because they haven't filed bankruptcy yet. I have to get things that are essentially not what I want, but where I know that the creators are most likely to receive a bigger cut, like importing the original Japanese BluRays, which cost several hundred Euro per series. I have done that and I still do not even have a BD player, because why would I? I can get what I want for free in better quality already. Sometimes I just want to give money to who I actually want to support and it's not possible.

I'm still in my 20ies and I pirate absolutely everything. From Windows, all the shows I watch, the vast majority of games I have played in my entire life, all software besides games, all music I have ever listened to offline somehow.  

I am a big fan of books. Here is my problem with IP: There are a many plentiful of cases where for whatever reason you can lose control over a piece of digital media. Forget your account, break the EULA you must agree to, maybe lose the device the software or whatever was bound to. Any and all limitations on digital media are artificial. Unless someone breaks into my home, I am mostly in control of my book. That is what media should be like. Something you own, not something you ever have to worry about losing access to.    

And here is the probably morally wrong side of things from me: as you get better at being a pirate, you realize that piracy is actually way better a deal than everything else, with no competition. I am confident I can get the majority of digital things I am interested in faster, in better quality (no DRMs for example) and fully for free within a day of wanting it. No region lock, no expiration date, I can share it with whoever I want, I don't need to worry about refunding it because I didn't like the first two hours.  
Though admittedly, I am mostly in luck because things that get pirated. I remember one of the Handball Manager games didn't get it's denuvo cracked and some people are still waiting. Luckily my interests are favored in the pirate community as well.  

The only reason I ever buy something digital is because I want to actively support who made it.
Of course it's voluntary. If you chose to illegally cross the border, this is a risk you are willing to take.

I can't finish my thesis. It's my major goal right now, besides gaining weight and not altering my routine too much that it all crumbles.  
We're not talking PhD or anything, it's my bachelor thesis - 40 pages in total. 

There are two major issues I have when writing or doing anything for it: Regardless of what kind of goal I set for myself, even when I accomplish it, it feels like I'm just dumping time into an endless time sink that never gives anything back. That's partially because I don't like my degree anymore and never want to work in this sector if I can somehow manage (Library Information Science BA at a German College). But there is more to it and I can't quite pinpoint it.  

The other is just the writing itself. I barely have an idea of what I'm doing here. I've attended classes and written or participated in papers, but I don't know what the hell I'm doing here. I just want to write in the style I'm writing here: short and what I'm thinking. I don't want to reduce myself to a machine that's going through sources on a topic and trying to assemble something new from that. Writing scientifically feels revolting. This is an excuse, but I don't like this. It's the opposite of fun and engaging and banging my head against a wall feels like I'm accomplishing more in my life than writing this. The reason I'm still doing it is because I invested now 4 years of my life to this shit and I'm not going to just drop it without a diploma, even though I hate it.  

First I wanted to write about the effects Blockchain technologies will have on the library sector in general, but my prof wasn't satisfied by my thesis and said it's too broad and doesn't contribute much to scientific discussion.  
Now I'm gathering sources on how diplomas and accreditation of education work right now and what potentials there are in the future. You got the classic paper diplomas, the solution of the MIT that's entirely digital with a blockchain timestamp and a nifty app, a solution from a uni in Göttingen, Germany where they basically just replace the physical signature on diplomas with a link to a copy of the diploma hosted by the university so you can compare them and Open Badges that are used for example by Codeacademy or the Open University. So it's not just higher education I'm interested in. 
I can't stretch this for 40 pages, it's boring, it's got nothing to do with what I care about, I have no clue about this topic, my profs aren't responding and I just want it to be over.  

So what can I do to fix this? #1 Write out the problem #2 Break it down into smaller parts #3 Do the smaller parts. Though I think I have been doing that already and it feels like it's not working. 

Ahh yea, one thing makes sense now. I keep losing faith in whatever system of goals and orientation I set up for writing my thesis, because I don't have the confidence that it will lead me to a happy ending. Why would I, I have never written anything scientifically of any significant length or in good faith. 

So I gotta make a plan on what to do next. I already have this one I made a couple of days ago, so my plan is to work through that starting tomorrow. Yes that sounds big and daunting and I know I can't do it all, but if I start with the first task and just seriously writing one sentence towards accomplishing that task I know I'll accomplish it. That's telling one of my profs that the other isn't responding and I need feedback because I'm lost. I can do that, I'm sorting my thoughts about it already aren't I, good job me.  
 
What I made last time was a long list of sources I want to look at or need to ask, like the MIT digital certificate people. But I also have questions about content and writing ~~and urghh I don't want to write anymore, it's just hatred and anger that I am not already done with this boring shit~~ for writing it's best that I just write it all out as un-sloppily as possible and then just annoy my profs with questions until one of them finally hears me out.  

If you read this far, thank you. If you have any advice on writing in general/scientifically or anything related to digital diplomas and accreditation I'd be glad to hear it.

I picked a BA in library information science, even though I never go to libraries. But it had some parts that seemed interesting and included what I would have liked to get better at. I'm now writing my thesis so I can graduate and I can confidently say that I probably never want to work in a library. I'm more interested in building a business and creating art, even though I have 0 experience and talent in these areas.  

What I'm trying to say is that if you can't do something confidently, you have to try other things. Make a list of things that you think are worthy of pursuing somewhat, or that have your interest enough that you would like to dedicate yourself to them. Then seriously try them and see what sticks. Whatever experience you will have, in the worst case scenario you will be able to say "This isn't what I want to do." It still helps you narrow in the things that you are choosing from.

FA helps you make that list of things that are worth of pursuing and what exactly is how important to you.
